動物號角具有原始而粗獷的音色質感，音質偏向暗沉而帶有野性特徵。其音域相對有限，多: The animal horn has a raw, rough timbre, on the dark side and with a wild character. Its range is fairly limited, mostly from the lower middle register to the middle, but its volume carries strongly. Because the material is animal horn, the inside forms a naturally irregular cavity, so the resonance is particular and nasal in colour, usually with pronounced overtones and harmonics. Against the clear, smooth sound of brass, the animal horn is coarser and more forceful; against woodwind, its resonance is deeper and more metallic. These qualities suit it above all for a raw, desolate or solemn atmosphere, and give it a voice of its own in regional music and ritual.
吹角最原始以牛科洞角或木製成，多在角尖開孔吹奏；歐洲最早發現為青銅時代金屬號角，: The blowing horn was at first made from a bovine horn or from wood, usually blown through a hole at the tip; the earliest found in Europe are Bronze Age metal horns, and the oldest surviving animal horn dates from the late Iron Age, from Vestnium in Sweden. Because Scandinavia has few large horned animals, horns there are commonly of wood, of rolled birch bark, or of the kind called a lur. Its uses grew from ancient signalling, warfare, hunting, religion and assembly: before the end of the sixteenth century a horn was blown from Basque mountain tops to call a meeting, and Inca messengers announced their arrival with a pututu. Early European horns also developed into Western brass, and Wagner's operas call for bovine horns with the tips removed.

Early Europe had Bronze Age horns of metal, and northern Europe, having few large horned animals, used wood, rolled birch bark or strips of wood to make the lur. Elsewhere there are bamboo and wood, hollowed timber, the old stems of macleaya, gourds, clay and plastic. A hollow horn is usually pierced at the tip or fitted with a tube, and some are pierced at the side; the source does not state the materials of the other parts.

A horn (a blowing horn or horn) is an aerophone made from a bovine horn or another material in the shape of a horn, Hornbostel–Sachs number 423.121.2. It is usually blown through a hole at the tip, and there are also forms with a hole in the side or a fitted tube. Because its pitch is fairly uniform, it is used mainly to carry signals, in warfare, herding, farming, hunting and fishing, religious rites, ceremonial processions and group identification; herding, farming and hunter-gatherer societies also keep its function. Its uses include Jewish rites, Tibetan Buddhist rites, the development of early European horns into Western brass instruments, and the plastic horn blown by modern football supporters.
